claim: Hungry flies prefer a lower temperature than fed flies.
source: When w1118 flies were starved overnight with water only, they preferred 21.7 ± 0.3°C (Figure 1D: overnight starvation (STV), gray bar). Thus, starvation leads to a lower Tp.
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays showing starved flies prefer 21.7°C compared to fed flies preferring 25.2°C

claim: Fed w1118 flies prefer a temperature of 25.2 ± 0.2°C.
source: The flies are released into a chamber set to a temperature range of 16–34°C and subsequently accumulate at their preferred temperature (Tp) at 25.2 ± 0.2°C within 30 min (Figure 1D: fed, white bar).
evidence: Direct measurement from temperature preference behavioral assays

claim: Refeeding starved flies with fly food for 10 minutes results in full recovery of temperature preference to fed state levels.
source: After 10 min, 30 min, or 1 hr of fly food refeeding, starved flies preferred a temperature similar to that of fed flies (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1: orange bar, statistics shown as red stars, Figure 1—source data 1), suggesting a full recovery from starvation.
evidence: Experimental data showing temperature preference after refeeding with fly food

claim: Refeeding starved flies with sucralose for 10 minutes results in partial recovery of temperature preference.
source: After starved flies were refed sucralose for 10 min or 1 hr, they preferred a warmer temperature; however, Tp was halfway between Tps of fed and starved flies (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1: blue bar, Figure 1—source data 1). Thus, sucralose ingestion induces a warm preference but shows a partial recovery of Tp from the starved state.
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays after sucralose refeeding

claim: Sucralose is a non-metabolizable sugar with no calories.
source: Importantly, sucralose is a non-metabolizable sugar and has no calories.
evidence: Established biochemical property of sucralose

claim: Sucralose activates sweet taste neurons in Drosophila.
source: Sucralose is an artificial sweetener that activates sweet taste neurons in Drosophila (Biolchini et al., 2017) and modulates taste behaviors such as the proboscis extension reflex (Park et al., 2017; Dahanukar et al., 2007; Dus et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Refeeding starved flies with glucose for 10 minutes results in full recovery of temperature preference.
source: We found that 10 min or 1 hr glucose refeeding resulted in full recovery of Tp from the starved state (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1: green bar, statistics shown in red NS, Figure 1—source data 1) and was significantly different from starved flies (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1: statistics shown in green stars, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays after glucose refeeding

claim: Starved flies touch glucose and sucralose at similar frequencies during feeding.
source: We found that starved flies touched glucose and sucralose food at similar frequencies and more frequently than water during the 30-min test period (Figure 1H, Figure 1—source data 1). The data suggest that flies are likely to feed on glucose and sucralose at similar rates.
evidence: Data from FLIC system feeding assays

claim: Refeeding starved flies with fructose for 10 minutes results in full recovery of temperature preference.
source: We found that 10 min of fructose refeeding resulted in full recovery of Tp from the starved state (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, purple bar: statistics shown in red NS, Figure 1—source data 1), and 10 min and 1 hr fructose refeeding were significantly different from starved flies (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1: statistics shown in green stars, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays after fructose refeeding

claim: Sweet taste is more important than sugar structure for temperature preference recovery.
source: The data suggest that sweet taste is more important than the structures of the sugar compounds.
evidence: Inference from comparison of glucose and fructose refeeding results

claim: Sweet gustatory receptor mutants (Gr5a−/−; Gr64a−/−) fail to show taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: However, starved sweet Gr mutant flies did not increase Tp after 10 min sucralose refeeding (Figure 2A, B, blue bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 2—source data 1). These data suggest that sweet Grs are involved in taste-evoked warm preference.
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays using sweet Gr mutants

claim: Sweet gustatory receptor mutants show normal starvation response.
source: We found that sweet Gr mutant flies exhibited a normal starvation response in which the Tp of starved flies was lower than that of fed flies (Figure 2A, B, white and gray bars, statistics shown as green stars, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays using sweet Gr mutants

claim: Silencing all sweet gustatory receptor neurons prevents taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: However, flies silencing all sweet GRNs failed to show a warm preference after 10 min of sucralose refeeding (Figure 2C, blue bar, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using Gr64f-Gal4>uas-Kir to silence sweet GRNs

claim: Optogenetic activation of all sweet gustatory receptor neurons induces a warm preference in starved flies.
source: Excitation of all sweet GRNs by red light pulses elicited a warm preference, and Tp was intermediate between fed and starved flies, suggesting partial recovery (Figure 2G, yellow bar, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using optogenetic activation with CsChrimson

claim: Optogenetic activation of Gr5a-expressing neurons alone does not induce a warm preference.
source: However, neither excitation of Gr5a- (Figure 2H) nor Gr64a-expressing neurons (Figure 2I) induced a warm preference (yellow bars, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using optogenetic activation with CsChrimson

claim: Optogenetic activation of Gr64a-expressing neurons alone does not induce a warm preference.
source: However, neither excitation of Gr5a- (Figure 2H) nor Gr64a-expressing neurons (Figure 2I) induced a warm preference (yellow bars, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using optogenetic activation with CsChrimson

claim: Sweet gustatory receptors are required for nutrient-induced warm preference after glucose refeeding.
source: We next asked whether the sweet Grs contribute to the nutrient-induced warm preference. We found that all these starved flies did not increase Tp after 10 min of glucose intake (Figure 2A–C, green bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays using sweet Gr mutants and silenced flies

claim: Sweet gustatory receptor mutants can recover temperature preference after fly food refeeding.
source: Notably, we found that flies increased Tp after 10 min of refeeding with fly food containing carbohydrate, fat, and protein (Figure 2A–C, orange bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays using sweet Gr mutants

claim: Anterior cells (ACs) are warm-sensing neurons involved in temperature preference behavior.
source: The warm-sensing neurons, anterior cells (ACs), and the cold-sensing R11F02-Gal4-expressing neurons control temperature preference behavior (Umezaki et al., 2018; Hamada et al., 2008; Ni et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Anterior cells control hunger-driven lower temperature preference.
source: We have previously shown that starved flies choose a lower Tp, the so-called hunger-driven lower Tp (Umezaki et al., 2018). ACs control the hunger-driven lower Tp, but cold-sensing R11F02-Gal4-expressing neurons do not (Umezaki et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Anterior cells express TrpA1, which responds to warm temperatures above 25°C.
source: ACs express transient receptor potential A1 (TrpA1), which responds to a warm temperature >25°C (Hamada et al., 2008; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Silencing anterior cells prevents taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: To examine whether ACs regulate taste-evoked warm preference, we refed sucralose to AC-silenced flies for 10 min. We found that the Tp of the refed flies was still similar to that of the starved flies (Figure 3A, blue bar, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 3—source data 1), indicating that sucralose refeeding could not restore Tp and that ACs are involved in taste-evoked warm preference.
evidence: Experimental data using TrpA1SH-Gal4>uas-Kir to silence ACs

claim: Silencing R11F02-Gal4-expressing cold-sensing neurons prevents taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: To determine whether R11F02-Gal4-expressing neurons are involved in taste-evoked warm preference, we silenced R11F02-Gal4-expressing neurons using uas-Kir. We found that the flies showed a significant difference in Tp between fed and starved conditions, but the flies did not show a warm preference upon sucralose refeeding (Figure 3B, gray and blue bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using R11F02-Gal4>uas-Kir to silence cold neurons

claim: Optogenetic activation of warm-sensing neurons increases temperature preference in starved flies.
source: To further ensure the results, we used optogenetics to artificially excite warm and cold neurons with TrpA1SH-Gal4 and R11F02-Gal4, respectively, by red light pulses for 10 min. We compared the Tp of starved flies with and without ATR under red light. Tp of starved flies with ATR was significantly increased (Figure 3F, G, yellow bars, statistics shown as black stars, Figure 3—source data 1) compared to those without ATR (Figure 3F, G, gray bars, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using optogenetic activation with CsChrimson

claim: Optogenetic activation of cold-sensing neurons increases temperature preference in starved flies.
source: To further ensure the results, we used optogenetics to artificially excite warm and cold neurons with TrpA1SH-Gal4 and R11F02-Gal4, respectively, by red light pulses for 10 min. We compared the Tp of starved flies with and without ATR under red light. Tp of starved flies with ATR was significantly increased (Figure 3F, G, yellow bars, statistics shown as black stars, Figure 3—source data 1) compared to those without ATR (Figure 3F, G, gray bars, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using optogenetic activation with CsChrimson

claim: Olfaction is involved in warm preference after sucralose refeeding in hungry flies.
source: We also investigated the potential effects of olfaction. We used mutants of the odorant receptor co-receptor, Orco (Orco1), which has an olfactory defect (Larsson et al., 2004). We found that the flies showed a significant difference in Tp between fed and starved conditions, but the flies did not show a warm preference upon sucralose refeeding (Figure 3H, gray and blue bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using Orco1 mutants

claim: NPF is the Drosophila homolog of mammalian NPY (neuropeptide Y).
source: Therefore, we first focused on neuropeptide F (NPF) and small neuropeptide F (sNPF), which are the Drosophila homolog and ortholog of mammalian NPY, respectively (Nässel and Wegener, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: sNPF is the Drosophila ortholog of mammalian NPY.
source: Therefore, we first focused on neuropeptide F (NPF) and small neuropeptide F (sNPF), which are the Drosophila homolog and ortholog of mammalian NPY, respectively (Nässel and Wegener, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Silencing DH44-expressing neurons prevents taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: We found that DH44- or AKH-expressing neuron silenced flies failed to show a taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding. However, they were able to increase Tp after 10 min glucose or fly food refeeding (Figure 4D, F, green and orange bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting a normal nutrient-induced warm preference.
evidence: Experimental data using Dh44-Gal4>uas-Kir

claim: Silencing AKH-expressing neurons prevents taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: We found that DH44- or AKH-expressing neuron silenced flies failed to show a taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding. However, they were able to increase Tp after 10 min glucose or fly food refeeding (Figure 4D, F, green and orange bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting a normal nutrient-induced warm preference.
evidence: Experimental data using Akh-Gal4>uas-Kir

claim: DH44 is the Drosophila homolog of mammalian corticotropin-releasing hormone.
source: The major hunger signals (Lin et al., 2019), diuretic hormone 44 (DH44), and adipokinetic hormone (AKH) are the mammalian corticotropin-releasing hormone homolog (Dus et al., 2015) and the functional glucagon homolog, respectively (Lee and Park, 2004; Kim and Rulifson, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: AKH is the functional glucagon homolog in Drosophila.
source: The major hunger signals (Lin et al., 2019), diuretic hormone 44 (DH44), and adipokinetic hormone (AKH) are the mammalian corticotropin-releasing hormone homolog (Dus et al., 2015) and the functional glucagon homolog, respectively (Lee and Park, 2004; Kim and Rulifson, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Ilp6 mutants fail to show taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: We found that the ilp6 loss-of-function (ilp6 LOF) mutant failed to show a taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding (Figure 4G, blue bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1), but did show a nutrient-induced warm preference after glucose refeeding (Figure 4G, green bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1). These data suggest that Ilp6 is required for taste-evoked warm preference but not for nutrient-induced warm preference after glucose or fly food refeeding.
evidence: Experimental data using ilp6 LOF mutants

claim: Ilp6 is a homolog of mammalian insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1).
source: Insulin-like peptide 6 (Ilp6) is a homolog of mammalian insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1), and ilp6 mRNA expression is increased in starved flies (Okamoto et al., 2009; Slaidina et al., 2009; Bai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: ilp6 mRNA expression is increased in starved flies.
source: Insulin-like peptide 6 (Ilp6) is a homolog of mammalian insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1), and ilp6 mRNA expression is increased in starved flies (Okamoto et al., 2009; Slaidina et al., 2009; Bai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: upd3 mutants fail to show taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: We found that the upd3 mutants failed to show a taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding (Figure 4H, blue bar, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1), but showed a nutrient-induced warm preference after glucose or normal food refeeding (Figure 4H, green and orange bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1). These data suggest that Upd3 is required for taste-evoked warm preference, but not for nutrient-induced warm preference after glucose or normal food refeeding.
evidence: Experimental data using upd3 mutants

claim: Upd3 is a Drosophila cytokine that is upregulated under nutritional stress.
source: Unpaired3 (Upd3) is a Drosophila cytokine that is upregulated under nutritional stress (Woodcock et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: upd2 mutants fail to show warm preference after refeeding with sucralose, glucose, or fly food.
source: The upd2 mutants failed to show a warm preference after refeeding of sucralose, glucose or fly food (Figure 4I, blue, green and orange bars, statistics shown as green and red stars, Figure 4—source data 1). Thus, our data suggest that factors involved in the hunger state are required for taste-evoked warm preference.
evidence: Experimental data using upd2 mutants

claim: Upd2 is a functional leptin homolog in Drosophila.
source: We also examined the role of the satiety factor Unpaired2 (Upd2), a functional leptin homolog in flies (Rajan and Perrimon, 2012), in taste-evoked warm preference.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Flies show rhythmic feeding patterns with peaks in the morning or morning and evening.
source: Flies show a rhythmic feeding pattern: one peak in the morning (Ro et al., 2014) or two peaks in the morning and evening (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Starved y1w1 flies show taste-evoked warm preference at all time points tested during the day.
source: While starved y1w1 flies showed a taste-evoked warm preference at all time points (Figure 5B1, gray and blue lines, Figure 5—source data 1), starved w1118 flies showed a significant taste-evoked warm preference at ZT4–6 and 10–12 (Figure 5A1, gray and blue lines, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays at different times of day

claim: Starved w1118 flies show significant taste-evoked warm preference at ZT4-6 and ZT10-12.
source: While starved y1w1 flies showed a taste-evoked warm preference at all time points (Figure 5B1, gray and blue lines, Figure 5—source data 1), starved w1118 flies showed a significant taste-evoked warm preference at ZT4–6 and 10–12 (Figure 5A1, gray and blue lines, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data from temperature preference assays at different times of day

claim: Clock gene mutants per01 and tim01 fail to show taste-evoked warm preference after sucralose refeeding.
source: Although they showed significant starvation responses (Figure 5C, D, black and gray lines, Figure 5—source data 1), neither starved per01 nor tim01 mutants could show taste-evoked warm preference upon sucralose refeeding (Figure 5C1, D1, blue lines, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Experimental data using per01 and tim01 mutants

claim: Clock gene mutants per01 and tim01 show full recovery of temperature preference after glucose refeeding.
source: Nevertheless, they fully recovered upon glucose refeeding in LD at any time of day (Figure 5C2, D2, green lines, Figure 5—source data 1). Therefore, our data suggest that clock genes are required for taste-evoked warm preference, but not for nutrient-induced warm preference.
evidence: Experimental data using per01 and tim01 mutants

claim: Starved per01 and tim01 mutants touch water significantly more often than glucose or sucralose.
source: Interestingly, starved per01 and tim01 mutants touched water significantly more often than glucose or sucralose (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Data from FLIC feeding assays

claim: Drosophila body temperature is close to ambient temperature due to their low mass as small ectotherms.
source: Due to the low mass of small ectotherms, the source of temperature comes from the environment. Therefore, their body temperatures are close to the ambient temperature (Stevenson, 1985a; Stevenson, 1985b).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Flies in lower environmental temperature have lower metabolic rate.
source: The flies in a lower environmental temperature has been shown to have a lower metabolic rate, and the flies in a higher environmental temperature has been shown to have a higher metabolic rate (Umezaki et al., 2018; Berrigan and Partridge, 1997; Schilman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Flies in higher environmental temperature have higher metabolic rate.
source: The flies in a lower environmental temperature has been shown to have a lower metabolic rate, and the flies in a higher environmental temperature has been shown to have a higher metabolic rate (Umezaki et al., 2018; Berrigan and Partridge, 1997; Schilman et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Starvation causes lower body temperature in mammals.
source: Similarly, in mammals, starvation causes a lower body temperature, hypothermia (Piccione et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Starved mammals have lower heat production.
source: The starved mammals have been shown a lower heat production (Keys et al., 1950; Piccione et al., 2002; Sakurada et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Cephalic phase response (CPR) in mammals involves physiological changes initiated by sensory detection of food before nutrient absorption.
source: Immediately after seeing, smelling, or chewing food, even without absorbing nutrients, a burst of physiological changes is suddenly initiated in the body. These responses are known in mammals as the cephalic phase response (CPR) (Smeets et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CPR in mammals includes increased saliva and gastrointestinal secretions to prepare for digestion.
source: For example, a flood of saliva and gastrointestinal secretions prepares hungry animals to digest food (Chen and Knight, 2016; Power and Schulkin, 2008; Zafra et al., 2006; Pavlov, 1902; Garrison and Knight, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Chewing food triggers rapid increase in heat production in mammals, demonstrating CPR in thermogenesis.
source: Starvation results in lower body temperatures, and chewing food triggers a rapid increase in heat production, demonstrating CPR in thermogenesis (LeBlanc, 2000; LeBlanc and Cabanac, 1989; LeBlanc et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Flies exhibit circadian rhythms of temperature preference (TPR).
source: For example, we have shown that preferred temperature increases during the daytime and decreases during the night time, exhibiting circadian rhythms of temperature preference (temperature preference rhythms: TPR) (Kaneko et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Temperature preference rhythms (TPR) in Drosophila lead to body temperature rhythms (BTR) similar to mammalian BTR.
source: Because their surrounding temperature is very close to their body temperature, TPR leads to body temperature rhythms (BTR) that is very similar to mammalian BTR (Goda and Hamada, 2019; Goda et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Taste-evoked warm preference in Drosophila may be a physiological response equivalent to CPR in mammals.
source: The taste-evoked warm preference in Drosophila may be a physiological response potentially equivalent to CPR in mammals.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of taste-evoked responses in flies and CPR in mammals

claim: Starvation recovery is controlled by two components: taste-evoked and nutrient-induced warm preferences.
source: The data suggest that starvation recovery is controlled by two components: taste-evoked and nutrient-induced warm preferences, and that taste and nutrient quality play distinct roles in starvation recovery.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing differential effects of sucralose and glucose

claim: Taste and nutrient quality play distinct roles in starvation recovery.
source: The data suggest that starvation recovery is controlled by two components: taste-evoked and nutrient-induced warm preferences, and that taste and nutrient quality play distinct roles in starvation recovery.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing differential effects of sucralose and glucose

claim: Clock genes profoundly control taste-evoked warm preferences.
source: We found that clock genes and hunger signals profoundly control the taste-evoked warm preferences.
evidence: Experimental data showing per01 and tim01 mutants fail to show taste-evoked warm preference

claim: Hunger signals profoundly control taste-evoked warm preferences.
source: We found that clock genes and hunger signals profoundly control the taste-evoked warm preferences.
evidence: Experimental data showing various hunger signal mutants fail to show taste-evoked warm preference

claim: Taste-evoked response represents internal energy homeostasis and metabolism.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the taste-evoked response is one of the critical layers of regulatory mechanisms representing internal energy homeostasis and metabolism.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing involvement of hunger signals and clock genes

claim: Both warm and cold neurons are important for taste-evoked warm preference.
source: The data suggest that both warm and cold neurons are important for taste-evoked warm preference: while ACs are required for the hunger-driven lower Tp (Umezaki et al., 2018), both ACs and cold neurons are likely to be important for this taste-evoked warm preference.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing both AC and cold neuron silencing prevent taste-evoked warm preference

claim: Taste-evoked warm preference is a rapid response compared to hunger-driven lower temperature preference.
source: The hunger-driven lower Tp is a slower response because starvation gradually lowers their Tp (Umezaki et al., 2018). In contrast, the taste-evoked warm preference is a rapid response.
evidence: Inference from comparison of time courses of different responses

claim: Taste-evoked warm preference and nutrient-induced warm preference differ at the internal state level but not at the sensory level.
source: Thus, taste-evoked warm preference and nutrient-induced warm preference differ at the internal state level, but not at the sensory level.
evidence: Inference from experimental data showing hunger signals affect taste-evoked but not nutrient-induced responses, while sensory signals affect both

claim: Hunger signaling hormones/peptides are important for taste modulation.
source: The hunger signaling hormones/peptides studied in this project are important for taste modulation. For example, mammalian NPY and its Drosophila homolog NPF modulate the output of taste signals (Wang et al., 2016; Inagaki et al., 2014; Herness and Zhao, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The AKH receptor is expressed in a subset of gustatory neurons.
source: The AKH receptor is expressed in a subset of gustatory neurons that may modulate taste information for carbohydrate metabolism (Bharucha et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Taste neurons express clock genes.
source: For example, taste neurons express clock genes, and impaired clock function in taste neurons disrupts daily rhythms in feeding behavior (Chatterjee et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Temperature-sensing neurons transmit temperature information to central clock neurons.
source: Temperature-sensing neurons transmit hot or cold temperature information to central clock neurons (Tang et al., 2017; Alpert et al., 2020; Marin et al., 2020; Yadlapalli et al., 2018; Jin et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DH44-expressing neurons are located in the pars intercerebralis of the fly brain.
source: DH44 is located in the dorsomedial region of the fly brain, the pars intercerebralis, and DH44-expressing neurons play a role in the output pathway of the central clock (King et al., 2017; Barber et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DH44-expressing neurons play a role in the output pathway of the central clock.
source: DH44 is located in the dorsomedial region of the fly brain, the pars intercerebralis, and DH44-expressing neurons play a role in the output pathway of the central clock (King et al., 2017; Barber et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Insulin-producing cells (IPCs) receive circadian and metabolic signals.
source: IPCs receive a variety of information, including circadian (Barber et al., 2021; Cavanaugh et al., 2014) and metabolic signals (Okamoto et al., 2009; Slaidina et al., 2009; Bai et al., 2012; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Upd2 and Ilp6 are expressed in the fat body and respond to metabolic states.
source: Both Upd2 and Ilp6, which are expressed in the fat body respond to metabolic states and remotely regulate Ilp expression (Okamoto et al., 2009; Slaidina et al., 2009; Bai et al., 2012; Rajan and Perrimon, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Insect fat body is analogous to fat tissues and liver in vertebrates.
source: Insect fat body is analogous to the fat tissues and liver in the vertebrates (Li et al., 2019; Arrese and Soulages, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: CPR is influenced by smell in mammals.
source: In fact, CPR is known to be influenced by smell as well in mammals (Chen and Knight, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: CPR allows flies to choose a more hospitable place to restore their physiological state.
source: CPR may allow flies to choose a more hospitable place to restore their physiological state and allow for a higher metabolism, and eventually move on to the next step, such as foraging and actively seeking a mate before competitors arrive.
evidence: Speculation about the adaptive function of CPR in flies

claim: CPR may be a strategy for the fly's survival.
source: Thus, CPR may be a strategy for the fly's survival.
evidence: Speculation about the adaptive function of CPR

claim: Circadian clocks control feeding behavior in part via orexigenic peptidergic/hormonal regulation.
source: Circadian clocks control feeding behavior in part via orexigenic peptidergic/hormonal regulation such as neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons, which are critical for regulating feeding and metabolism (Hirayama et al., 2018; Blasiak et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Feeding-fasting cycles modulate peripheral organs in liver, gut, and pancreas.
source: Feeding–fasting cycles modulate peripheral organs in liver, gut, pancreas, and so on (Panda, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Daily feeding timing influences energy homeostasis and metabolism.
source: Daily feeding timing influences energy homeostasis and metabolism (Greenhill, 2018; Chaix et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Circadian clock drives daily feeding rhythms.
source: The circadian clock drives daily feeding rhythms (Cedernaes et al., 2019; Longo and Panda, 2016; Hirayama et al., 2018) and anticipates meal timing.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Intracerebroventricular injection of NPY induces CPR in mammals.
source: While intracerebroventricular injection of NPY induces the CPR (Geoghegan et al., 1993), injection of NPY antagonists suppresses CPR in dogs, suggesting that NPY is a regulator of CPR in mammals (Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: NPY antagonists suppress CPR in dogs.
source: While intracerebroventricular injection of NPY induces the CPR (Geoghegan et al., 1993), injection of NPY antagonists suppresses CPR in dogs, suggesting that NPY is a regulator of CPR in mammals (Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: NPY is a regulator of CPR in mammals.
source: While intracerebroventricular injection of NPY induces the CPR (Geoghegan et al., 1993), injection of NPY antagonists suppresses CPR in dogs, suggesting that NPY is a regulator of CPR in mammals (Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: Inference from experimental data cited from prior research

claim: Flies have sensory neurons that detect fatty acids.
source: Because flies have sensory neurons that detect fatty acids (Masek and Keene, 2013; Ahn et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2021) or amino acids (Croset et al., 2016; Ganguly et al., 2017; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017; Steck et al., 2018), these neurons may drive the response to fly food intake.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Flies have sensory neurons that detect amino acids.
source: Because flies have sensory neurons that detect fatty acids (Masek and Keene, 2013; Ahn et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2021) or amino acids (Croset et al., 2016; Ganguly et al., 2017; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017; Steck et al., 2018), these neurons may drive the response to fly food intake.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Fatty acid or amino acid sensing neurons may drive the response to fly food intake in sweet-insensitive flies.
source: Because flies have sensory neurons that detect fatty acids (Masek and Keene, 2013; Ahn et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2021) or amino acids (Croset et al., 2016; Ganguly et al., 2017; Chen and Dahanukar, 2017; Steck et al., 2018), these neurons may drive the response to fly food intake. This is likely why the sweet-insensitive flies can still recover after eating fly food (Figure 2A–C, orange bars).
